screens.title: Network Troubleshooting on Linux
screens.narratorSegment: Network problems on Linux usually hide in one of a few places: basic reachability, interface settings, listening services, DNS name resolution, or firewall rules. In this lesson you'll learn a systematic workflow that moves from the physical and link layers up to DNS and security, so you can avoid jumping to conclusions. For example, you will learn to use ping to prove basic reachability, traceroute to find the hop that fails, ip and ifconfig to verify IP and gateway settings, ss or netstat to confirm a service is listening on a port, dig or nslookup for DNS checks, and firewalld or ufw commands to inspect firewall rules safely. Each tool gives a different kind of evidence; together they form a reliable diagnostic path. We'll also emphasise safety when changing firewall rules remotely and show how simple checks can prevent lockouts. By the end you'll have a repeatable checklist for troubleshooting web servers and other services on Linux. Think about the last time a host was "down" — was it really the host, or a blocked port or wrong DNS entry?

screens.title: A systematic troubleshooting workflow
screens.narratorSegment: A predictable sequence saves time and prevents errors. Begin by verifying basic reachability; if you can ping an IP address but not a hostname, you immediately know DNS is suspect. If you can't even ping an IP, the problem is lower in the stack — cabling, link, interface, or routing. After reachability, check the system's network interface settings and route table with ip addr show and ip route show to confirm IP, netmask, and default gateway. Then confirm the service is listening with ss -tulnp or netstat -tulnp so you know whether the application is reachable on the expected port. Next, check DNS using dig or nslookup if hostnames fail. Finally, inspect firewall rules with firewalld or ufw. A common misconception is to change firewall rules first; instead, use them last after you've ruled out other causes. For example, if a web host returns no response, run ping to 8.8.8.8, ip route show to verify default gateway, ss to confirm a server is listening on port 80, dig to verify the hostname resolves, and then firewall-cmd or ufw status to ensure ports allowed. This sequence narrows the problem quickly and reduces configuration churn. What step will you run first when a server appears offline?

content.html:
Core Concept
A systematic troubleshooting workflow
Follow a bottom-up sequence to isolate network faults
Step-by-step checklist
1. Verify reachability
Use ping to an IP, then a hostname to spot DNS problems.
2. Inspect interface & routing
ip addr show, ip route show to check IP, mask, and gateway.
3. Confirm listening services
ss -tulnp to list listening ports and owning processes.
4. Diagnose DNS
dig or nslookup to inspect resolver responses and servers used.
5. Verify firewall rules
Use firewalld or ufw status commands and only apply permanent rules after testing.
Example flow
# 1: test network path
ping -c 3 8.8.8.8
ping -c 3 google.com
# 2: check interface & route
ip addr show eth0
ip route show
# 3: confirm service
sudo ss -tulnp | grep :80
# 4: DNS troubleshooting
dig google.com
# 5: check firewall
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all
sudo ufw status verbose
Key Takeaway
A consistent sequence reduces diagnostic time and prevents unnecessary changes.
Common mistake
Changing firewall rules first often hides the real cause and can create new problems.
Check your understanding
If ping to 8.8.8.8 works but ping to google.com fails, what is the most likely next command?

screens.title: Using ping to verify basic connectivity
screens.narratorSegment: Ping is the quickest way to show whether a host is reachable at the IP layer. It sends ICMP echo requests and reports round-trip time. Start by pinging a known IP like 8.8.8.8 to confirm basic path connectivity independent of DNS. If that succeeds, ping a hostname next; if the hostname fails but the IP worked, DNS is likely at fault. Be aware some hosts or firewalls block ICMP, which is a common misconception — a failed ping doesn't always mean the host is down. Also, when ping succeeds but an application still fails, ping only confirms network reachability, not that the service is listening. Example commands include ping -c 3 8.8.8.8 and ping -c 3 google. com. Interpret the timing and packet-loss fields: high latency or packet loss points to network congestion or an unreliable link. Practice reading the output until you can quickly separate connectivity issues from DNS or service problems. After using ping, you'll know whether to continue up the stack with traceroute or inspect interface and routing settings. Using ping to verify basic connectivity means ping shows ip reachability; it does not prove an application is listening and some hosts may block icmp.. In practical terms, icmp echo as a first proof-of-life test. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Using ping to verify basic connectivity
ICMP echo as a first proof-of-life test
Command examples
ping -c 3 8.8.8.8
# checks IP reachability

ping -c 3 google.com
# checks DNS plus reachability
Example
If ping to 8.8.8.8 works but ping to google.com fails, dig into DNS settings next.
Misconception
Hosts may block ICMP; a failed ping does not always mean the server is offline.
Reading ping output
  • Packet loss indicates dropped packets or filtering between source and destination.
  • High round-trip times suggest congestion or a distant route.
  • Consistent success to an IP but not a name points to DNS problems.
Key Takeaway

Use ping to prove a basic IP path exists, then escalate to traceroute or DNS checks based on results.

screens.title: Traceroute for path diagnosis
screens.narratorSegment: Traceroute reveals each hop packets take to reach a destination, which helps you locate where connectivity breaks. On some distributions tracepath is available as an alternative. When you run traceroute to a hostname or IP, you’ll see a list of routers with round-trip times for each hop. If traceroute shows a failure at a particular hop, the issue is likely between your host and that hop — for example, a misconfigured router or ISP problem. Use traceroute to distinguish local network failures from upstream outages. Remember that intermediate routers may deprioritize or block traceroute probes, producing timeouts that don't necessarily mean the final host is unreachable. A practical sequence is: if ping to IP fails, run traceroute to see the last responding hop; if that hop is within your network, inspect local switches and routes; if it's outside, contact the upstream network. Practice reading traceroute output so you can tell whether a gap is on your LAN, your gateway, or further on the internet. Traceroute for path diagnosis means traceroute shows the path and where packets stop so you can focus troubleshooting on the correct network segment.. In practical terms, find where packets stop and measure hop latency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Core Concept
Traceroute for path diagnosis
Find where packets stop and measure hop latency
Command example
traceroute google.com
# or on some systems
tracepath google.com
Interpreting results
  • Each line shows a hop and sample RTTs; * indicates a timeout.
  • Timeouts on intermediate hops may be filtering, not necessarily final failure.
  • Look for the last responding hop inside your network to isolate local problems.
Scenario example
Example
If traceroute stops at your gateway, check its routes and connected links. If it fails outside your gateway, the fault is upstream.
Key Takeaway

Use traceroute to map the path and target the correct team or device when packets stop.

screens.title: Inspecting network interfaces with ip and ifconfig
screens.narratorSegment: Once you've verified reachability, confirm the machine's own interface configuration. The modern command is ip; ip addr show displays configured addresses and link state, while ip route show reveals the routing table and default gateway. ifconfig is older but still used on many systems. Look for an interface that is UP with a valid IP and the expected netmask. A common mistake is assuming the interface name is always eth0; modern systems often use different naming schemes. If an interface is DOWN, bring it up with sudo ip link set up and then re-check IP assignment and routes. Incorrect subnet masks or a missing default gateway are frequent causes of being able to reach hosts on the same subnet but not the internet. For example, ip addr show eth0 and ip route show should show a default route like default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0. If the default route is missing, add it or correct DHCP settings. Confirming these basics prevents wasted time chasing higher-layer symptoms. Inspecting network interfaces with ip and ifconfig means ensure interfaces are up, have correct ip and netmask, and that a default gateway exists to reach off-subnet destinations.. In practical terms, confirm ips, netmasks, and link status. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Inspecting network interfaces with ip and ifconfig
Confirm IPs, netmasks, and link status
Commands to know
ip addr show eth0
ip route show
# legacy
ifconfig -a
sudo ip link set eth0 up
Example
A missing default route explains why you can reach local hosts but not the internet.
Common inspection checklist
  • Is the interface state UP or DOWN?
  • Does the IP address match the expected subnet and netmask?
  • Is there a default route pointing to the correct gateway?
  • If DHCP is used, did it successfully assign an address?
Key Takeaway

Confirm interface state, addressing, and the default route before changing services or firewall rules.

screens.title: Bringing interfaces up and common interface issues
screens.narratorSegment: Some outages are caused by a downed interface or incorrect auto-configuration. If an interface shows DOWN, you can bring it up with sudo ip link set eth0 up. If the interface is up but has no IP, check DHCP or static configuration. A classic error is a wrong subnet mask that places the machine on a different logical network, preventing communication with expected peers. Another scenario is naming differences: modern systems may use predictable interface names rather than eth0, so always read ip addr show to find the actual name. When working remotely, avoid disabling an interface without console access. If DHCP assigns an unexpected address, check the DHCP server and lease settings. Use ip route show to ensure the default gateway is present; if not, add a route temporarily to test connectivity then correct persistent settings. The safe approach is to test changes locally or via a secondary management path to avoid being locked out. After correcting link or addressing issues, re-run ping and traceroute to confirm the path. Bringing interfaces up and common interface issues means interfaces can be up but misnamed or misconfigured; always verify names, ips, and routes before changing firewall or services.. In practical terms, fix simple link-state and addressing problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Core Concept
Bringing interfaces up and common interface issues
Fix simple link-state and addressing problems
Quick fixes
# bring interface up
sudo ip link set eth0 up

# check addresses and routes
ip addr show
ip route show

# add temporary default route
sudo ip route add default via 192.168.1.1
Troubleshooting checklist
  • Confirm the interface name and state with ip addr show.
  • Verify the IP and netmask match your expected subnet.
  • Ensure a default gateway exists for off-subnet traffic.
  • Avoid permanent changes before testing when working remotely.
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Finding listening services with ss and netstat
screens.narratorSegment: When a service isn't responding, the next question is whether it is actually listening on the expected port. The ss command is the modern tool for socket statistics; ss -tulnp lists listening TCP and UDP sockets with PIDs and program names when run with sudo. netstat -tulnp offers similar output on older systems. Use a filter such as sudo ss -tulnp | grep :80 to check HTTP or :443 for HTTPS. If nothing is listening on the expected port, the problem is the service configuration or it failed to start. If another process is listening, you have a port conflict. A common mistake is running ss without sudo and missing process names in the output. Another pitfall is assuming a listening process is reachable if it binds only to localhost; check whether services bind to 0.0.0.0 or a specific interface. Confirm both the port and the bind address, because binding to loopback prevents external connections even though the process is running. After confirming listeners, you can test connectivity from a client host or use curl or telnet to validate the application layer.

keyIdea.title: Listen vs. reachable
keyIdea.text: A process must be listening on the expected port and bound to an address reachable by clients; use ss or netstat to confirm both port and bind address.

content.html:
Core Concept
Finding listening services with ss and netstat
Confirm processes are bound to expected ports
Commands
sudo ss -tulnp
# filter for HTTP
sudo ss -tulnp | grep :80

# legacy
sudo netstat -tulnp
Example
If ss shows nginx listening on 127.0.0.1:80, external hosts cannot reach it. Reconfigure to bind to 0.0.0.0 or the needed interface.
Checks and interpretations

  • Check both port number and bind address (localhost vs. 0.0.0.0).
  • If nothing listens, inspect service logs and start the service.

Confirm a process listens on the correct port and is bound to an externally reachable address before checking firewalls or clients.

screens.title: Diagnosing DNS with dig and nslookup
screens.narratorSegment: DNS failures often masquerade as network outages. Use dig or nslookup to query DNS servers directly and inspect the answers returned. Run dig google. com and inspect the ANSWER SECTION to confirm the resolved IP and the SERVER line to see which resolver provided it. If dig returns SERVFAIL or no answer, check /etc/resolv. conf on the host to ensure nameserver entries are valid. If /etc/resolv. conf points to an unreachable DNS server, hostnames won't resolve even though IP paths work. A useful sequence: if ping to IP succeeds but ping to hostname fails, run dig for that hostname and verify the resolver and answer. Misinterpretation is common: seeing an IP in a browser does not prove DNS is correct for other hostnames; DNS records may be missing or wrong for specific names. Also check cache or local hosts files. After fixing DNS entries or resolver settings, test again by pinging the hostname to confirm full resolution and connectivity. Diagnosing DNS with dig and nslookup means use dig or nslookup to verify both the resolver used and the answers returned; check /etc/resolv.conf when resolution fails.. In practical terms, separate name resolution from network path problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Inspecting firewall rules with firewalld and ufw
screens.narratorSegment: Firewalls are often the final reason a service is unreachable. On RHEL-family systems firewalld is common; use sudo firewall-cmd --list-all to see active zones and open ports. On Debian-family systems ufw status verbose shows rules and status. If the required service or port, such as HTTP or HTTPS, isn’t listed, add a rule and test. For example, sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=http --permanent followed by sudo firewall-cmd --reload opens HTTP in firewalld. But be cautious: when working remotely via SSH, you can lock yourself out by applying restrictive rules. A safe practice is to add temporary rules first and confirm connectivity before making them permanent. Another tip is to check if the firewall blocks ICMP, which may explain ping failures even when services are reachable. A common misconception is to blame firewall immediately; instead, use it as the last check after confirming interfaces, routes, and listening services. Always test connectivity after each change and have a rollback or console access plan. Inspecting firewall rules with firewalld and ufw means inspect and test firewall rules carefully; use temporary rules and verification to avoid locking out remote access.. In practical terms, check before you change, and test rules safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Practical tips and common pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: A few practical habits make troubleshooting safer and faster. Always start with an IP ping to separate path problems from DNS. Run commands with sudo when you need process and PID information. When inspecting listeners, confirm the bind address; a service bound to localhost won't accept external traffic. For firewalls, prefer adding temporary rules and testing before making permanent changes, and ensure SSH is still allowed before you reload rules. Save outputs for comparison — copying ip, ss, dig, and firewall outputs into a note helps you see what changed after a configuration edit. Avoid assumptions about interface names; read the actual name with ip addr show. Finally, when a ping or traceroute shows timeouts at intermediate hops, consider that some routers de-prioritize such probes; don't conclude the final host is down without other evidence. Build these habits into your workflow and they will reduce accidental outages and speed up recovery. Practical tips and common pitfalls means use sudo when needed, test temporary firewall rules, verify bind addresses, and record outputs to compare before and after changes.. fullNarratorScript:
Network problems on Linux usually hide in one of a few places: basic reachability, interface settings, listening services, DNS name resolution, or firewall rules. In this lesson you'll learn a systematic workflow that moves from the physical and link layers up to DNS and security, so you can avoid jumping to conclusions. For example, you will learn to use ping to prove basic reachability, traceroute to find the hop that fails, ip and ifconfig to verify IP and gateway settings, ss or netstat to confirm a service is listening on a port, dig or nslookup for DNS checks, and firewalld or ufw commands to inspect firewall rules safely. Each tool gives a different kind of evidence; together they form a reliable diagnostic path. We'll also emphasise safety when changing firewall rules remotely and show how simple checks can prevent lockouts. By the end you'll have a repeatable checklist for troubleshooting web servers and other services on Linux. Think about the last time a host was "down" — was it really the host, or a blocked port or wrong DNS entry?

These objectives give you practical, verifiable skills. First, you'll verify basic network connectivity with ping and traceroute so you can tell whether a host is reachable and where packets stop. Second, you'll inspect network interfaces and routing using ip and ifconfig commands to confirm IP addresses, netmasks, and the default gateway. Third, you'll identify open ports and the processes that own them with ss or netstat, allowing you to confirm whether a service really listens on the expected port. Fourth, you'll use dig and nslookup to diagnose DNS resolution problems so you can separate DNS issues from network path problems. Each skill maps to real tasks: proving a server responds to ICMP, finding a misconfigured gateway, discovering a port conflict, or identifying a missing DNS record. Being able to perform and interpret each check quickly reduces downtime and narrows where you need to change configuration. Practice each command until its output becomes familiar — the numbers and names tell the true story behind an outage.

Beyond running commands, you must apply a careful workflow and safety practices. One objective here is to inspect and manage firewall rules using firewalld or ufw without locking yourself out while working remotely. Another objective is to adopt a systematic, bottom-up approach: verify connectivity first, then interfaces, then services, then DNS, then firewall. You'll also learn to validate fixes by re-running the same checks and interpreting the differences in outputs. Finally, the lab objective is to simulate and recover from a real web server connectivity issue using the full toolchain so you can practice the sequence until it becomes routine. These skills matter because hurried changes often cause more outages; a reproducible diagnostic sequence and safe rule changes reduce risk and save time. Learning Objectives — Practice and Safety means combine diagnostic commands with a controlled workflow and safety checks so troubleshooting does not create new problems.. In practical terms, skills for safe troubleshooting and lab verification. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A predictable sequence saves time and prevents errors. Begin by verifying basic reachability; if you can ping an IP address but not a hostname, you immediately know DNS is suspect. If you can't even ping an IP, the problem is lower in the stack — cabling, link, interface, or routing. After reachability, check the system's network interface settings and route table with ip addr show and ip route show to confirm IP, netmask, and default gateway. Then confirm the service is listening with ss -tulnp or netstat -tulnp so you know whether the application is reachable on the expected port. Next, check DNS using dig or nslookup if hostnames fail. Finally, inspect firewall rules with firewalld or ufw. A common misconception is to change firewall rules first; instead, use them last after you've ruled out other causes. For example, if a web host returns no response, run ping to 8.8.8.8, ip route show to verify default gateway, ss to confirm a server is listening on port 80, dig to verify the hostname resolves, and then firewall-cmd or ufw status to ensure ports allowed. This sequence narrows the problem quickly and reduces configuration churn. What step will you run first when a server appears offline?

Ping is the quickest way to show whether a host is reachable at the IP layer. It sends ICMP echo requests and reports round-trip time. Start by pinging a known IP like 8.8.8.8 to confirm basic path connectivity independent of DNS. If that succeeds, ping a hostname next; if the hostname fails but the IP worked, DNS is likely at fault. Be aware some hosts or firewalls block ICMP, which is a common misconception — a failed ping doesn't always mean the host is down. Also, when ping succeeds but an application still fails, ping only confirms network reachability, not that the service is listening. Example commands include ping -c 3 8.8.8.8 and ping -c 3 google. com. Interpret the timing and packet-loss fields: high latency or packet loss points to network congestion or an unreliable link. Practice reading the output until you can quickly separate connectivity issues from DNS or service problems. After using ping, you'll know whether to continue up the stack with traceroute or inspect interface and routing settings. Using ping to verify basic connectivity means ping shows ip reachability; it does not prove an application is listening and some hosts may block icmp.. In practical terms, icmp echo as a first proof-of-life test. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Traceroute reveals each hop packets take to reach a destination, which helps you locate where connectivity breaks. On some distributions tracepath is available as an alternative. When you run traceroute to a hostname or IP, you’ll see a list of routers with round-trip times for each hop. If traceroute shows a failure at a particular hop, the issue is likely between your host and that hop — for example, a misconfigured router or ISP problem. Use traceroute to distinguish local network failures from upstream outages. Remember that intermediate routers may deprioritize or block traceroute probes, producing timeouts that don't necessarily mean the final host is unreachable. A practical sequence is: if ping to IP fails, run traceroute to see the last responding hop; if that hop is within your network, inspect local switches and routes; if it's outside, contact the upstream network. Practice reading traceroute output so you can tell whether a gap is on your LAN, your gateway, or further on the internet. Traceroute for path diagnosis means traceroute shows the path and where packets stop so you can focus troubleshooting on the correct network segment.. In practical terms, find where packets stop and measure hop latency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Once you've verified reachability, confirm the machine's own interface configuration. When a service isn't responding, the next question is whether it is actually listening on the expected port. The ss command is the modern tool for socket statistics; ss -tulnp lists listening TCP and UDP sockets with PIDs and program names when run with sudo. netstat -tulnp offers similar output on older systems. If another process is listening, you have a port conflict. A common mistake is running ss without sudo and missing process names in the output.
